313.title: Everyone has gone astray (Romans 1:18–3:20)
313.hook: Paul argues that Jew and Gentile alike have missed the mark
313.howItsDone: Many Christians begin worship with a confession of sin said together, and many examine their day in the evening, naming where they fell short before asking God's forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul introduced himself to a church in Rome he had never met, and your line was not ashamed. Did you introduce yourself kindly to someone new? Day three hundred thirteen.

You know the group chat where someone starts listing everything wrong with everybody else. The coworker who never refills the coffee. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven. Everyone piles on, and it feels good. Then one friend types a single line: you do that too. Silence. Paul does exactly this to his readers in Rome. For a chapter and a half he describes a world that has turned away from God: greed, envy, gossip, cruelty, people who know better and don't care. You can almost hear the listeners nodding. Yes. Them. And then he turns around and points at the one nodding. Today's word is the one he's building toward.
screen: `A LIST OF EVERYONE ELSE'S WRONGS.` → `THE LISTENERS NOD.` → `THEN PAUL TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn, in the King James Bible: "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." Whoever you are. The finger that was pointing out now points back. Paul builds his case in two halves. First, the nations who never had the law of Moses. They still had creation, he says: God's power can be seen in the things that are made. And they still had a conscience, a law written on the heart, that sometimes accuses and sometimes excuses. Second, his own people, the Jewish people, who had the law and the promises. Paul is a Jew himself, arguing as an insider, and he says having the law is a gift, but hearing it isn't the same as keeping it. Then he lands the point with a string of lines, mostly from the Psalms: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down. Now the word. In Greek, the word Paul uses for sin is hamartia. Its verb, in older Greek, could mean to miss: a spear thrown that falls short of the target. So sin, for Paul, is not only a list of bad deeds. It's a condition everyone shares, a whole aim that's off. Christians describe how deep that goes in different ways, and we'll meet those differences in the days ahead. But on this much they agree: Paul isn't sorting the world into good people and bad people. He's putting everyone in the same room. And that's where the good news can start.
screen: `WHOSOEVER THOU ART THAT JUDGEST.` · `CREATION AND CONSCIENCE.` · `THE LAW, HEARD AND NOT KEPT.` · `HAMARTIA: MISSING THE MARK.` · then, large: `THERE IS NONE RIGHTEOUS, NO, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one way you missed the mark. Settle, and breathe. Let yesterday play back slowly, like a video. Somewhere in it, you aimed at kindness, or patience, or honesty, and fell a little short. Don't hunt for the worst thing you've ever done. Just find one small, real miss. Name it plainly, without a speech in your own defense and without beating yourself up. Then notice: whoever you judged this week has missed too, and so have you. Same room. If you pray, you can bring that one miss to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Sin. Hamartia in Greek, a word that could mean missing the mark. For Paul, not just bad deeds but a condition everyone shares.
Your line: all of us. Today, the next time you catch yourself judging someone, finish the sentence honestly: and I do that too. Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: But now (Romans 3:21–26)
314.hook: the hinge: all have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace
314.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize Romans 3:23–24 together, and Protestant churches in particular preach on it at the Reformation's anniversary each October, while Catholic and Orthodox teaching reads it alongside baptism and a lifelong healing by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sin, hamartia, missing the mark, and your line was all of us. When you caught yourself judging, did you finish the sentence: and I do that too? Day three hundred fourteen.

Think of a door on its hinge. The hinge is a small piece of metal, and the whole door swings on it. Paul's letter to the Romans has a hinge, and it's two words long. For almost three chapters he has been building a case that sounds like a courtroom closing argument. The nations without the law: guilty. His own people with the law: guilty too. Every mouth stopped, he says. The whole world stands in the dock. You can feel the gavel coming down. And then, right where the verdict should be, Paul writes two little words, and the whole letter swings open. Those two words are today.
screen: `A DOOR SWINGS ON A HINGE.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IN THE DOCK.` → `THEN TWO LITTLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested." But now. In Greek, nuni de. Everything before this was the bad news, laid out carefully. Everything after is the good news. And Paul doesn't take back a word of the bad news. He says it again, the most famous version: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." All. Nobody is let off. But the very next line is just as wide: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." Notice the pattern. The same all who fell short are the all who are offered grace. Now three words to open. Justified comes from the courtroom. In Greek it's about being declared in the right, set right with the judge. Freely is the Greek word for a gift, something you don't pay for. It's the same word John's Gospel uses when Jesus says they hated him without a cause: for nothing. And grace, charis, means favor you didn't earn. Christians have argued about this passage for five hundred years, so here's who says what. Many Protestants, following Luther, hear justified mainly as a verdict: God declares the guilty person righteous, as a gift received by faith. Catholics and Orthodox Christians tend to stress that God's grace also makes a person righteous, healing and changing them over a lifetime. In 1999, Lutheran and Catholic leaders signed a joint statement saying they share a basic understanding of it, while some differences remain. What no one disputes is the hinge. The story doesn't end at all have sinned. It turns on but now.
screen: `NUNI DE: BUT NOW.` · `ALL HAVE SINNED.` · `JUSTIFIED FREELY, AS A GIFT.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · then, large: `BUT NOW THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say but now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that feels like a final verdict about you. A thing you did. A label you've carried. A sentence that begins I'm the kind of person who. Let it be there, honestly. Don't argue with it. Then, on an out-breath, say quietly: but now. Say it again on the next breath. You're not erasing what happened. You're letting the story keep going past it. If you pray, you can hold that verdict before God and leave the next line to God. The bell holds the time.
But now. Nuni de in Greek. The hinge of Romans, where the verdict of all have sinned swings open into grace.
Your line: but now. Today, when an old mistake comes back to accuse you, let it finish its sentence, then add two words of your own: but now. Day three hundred fourteen.

original.note: Greek: but now. two small words that turn the whole letter.

315.title: Abraham believed (Romans 4)
315.hook: Abraham trusted God and it was counted as righteousness
315.howItsDone: Christians often point to Abraham as the model of faith, and many pray by naming a specific worry and entrusting it to God, sometimes with the words of a psalm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hinge of Romans, two words, and your line was but now. When an old mistake came back to accuse you, did you add those two words? Day three hundred fifteen.

Picture an old man standing outside his tent at night. He's close to a hundred. His wife is about ninety. They have no children, and by every sensible measure they never will. And God takes him outside and says: look up, count the stars if you can. So shall your descendants be. That's the scene in Genesis. Now picture Paul, centuries later, in the middle of his big argument about grace, and he needs one example everyone in Rome respects, Jew and Gentile alike. He doesn't pick a king or a prophet. He goes back to that old man under the stars. Today's word is what Abraham did there.
screen: `AN OLD MAN UNDER THE STARS.` → `COUNT THEM, IF YOU CAN.` → `PAUL GOES BACK TO ABRAHAM.`

segments.voice: Paul quotes Genesis, in the King James Bible: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." Two words to open. First, believed. The Greek noun behind it is pistis, faith, and it means trust more than opinion. Abraham didn't agree to a list of ideas. He leaned his whole weight on a promise. Second, counted. That's an accountant's word in Greek: credited, entered in the ledger. Abraham's trust was written into his account as being in the right with God. Then Paul makes a sharp point about timing. In Genesis, this verse comes before Abraham is circumcised, before the covenant sign. So, Paul says, Abraham is the father of everyone who trusts like this: his own people, and the nations too. And Paul doesn't pretend it was easy. He says Abraham looked honestly at his own body, as good as dead at about a hundred, and at Sarah's, and still trusted. "Who against hope believed in hope." Genesis is honest too: Abraham and Sarah both laugh at the promise at different moments, and they try a plan of their own along the way. Faith, in this story, is not the absence of doubt. It's trusting anyway. Christians read this chapter alongside the letter of James, which also points to Abraham and says faith without works is dead. Many Protestants hear Paul and James as two sides of one coin; Catholic and Orthodox teaching says much the same, stressing that living trust shows itself in deeds. And Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith. It's been a week of big words: grace, sin, but now. Today it comes down to one old man, looking up, trusting.
screen: `PISTIS: TRUST, NOT OPINION.` · `COUNTED: CREDITED TO HIS ACCOUNT.` · `BEFORE THE SIGN, FATHER OF ALL.` · `AGAINST HOPE, BELIEVED IN HOPE.` · then, large: `ABRAHAM BELIEVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust God with one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're gripping tightly right now. A test result. A child far away. Money. A decision you keep replaying. Hold it in your mind like something in your fist. Look at it honestly, the way Abraham looked at his own old body. Then, slowly, open your hand. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God and leave it there for the length of this sit. If you don't pray, simply loosen your grip for two minutes and notice what happens in your chest. The bell holds the time.
Faith. Pistis in Greek: trust, leaning your weight on a promise. Abraham's was counted to him as righteousness.
Your line: counted as right. Today, when you catch yourself gripping that one thing again, open your hand once more, and look up at the sky, even for a second. Day three hundred fifteen.
